$description: Semantic colour tokens. GENERATED by scripts/generate_semantic.py. Names are identical across every theme; only the alias target changes.

page.$description: the page itself. White in light, true black in dark - the user's own shipping value.

subtle.$description: a quietly differentiated region on the page

default.$description: cards and panels. NOTE the asymmetry, and it is deliberate: in LIGHT mode a card is the SAME white as the page and is separated by its border - that is what borders-over-shadows means, and it is what their references actually do. In DARK mode a card is LIGHTER than the page, because shadows do not register on black and lightness has to carry elevation instead. This is why dark mode is authored as a second value set and never as an inversion.

active.$description: a surface being pressed or selected

raised.$description: popovers, menus, dialogs. Lighter again in dark mode - one more elevation step.

raisedHover.$description: a row or control being hovered ON a raised surface. surface.hover cannot do this job in dark mode: it resolves to neutral 4, which is DARKER than surface.raised at neutral 5, so a menu item hovered on a popover got quieter instead of louder and surface.active is the same value as the surface itself. Elevation reverses the direction a hover has to move in, which is exactly why dark mode is authored rather than inverted, and why the raised layer needs its own pair.

raisedActive.$description: a row or control being pressed on a raised surface

sunken.$description: wells, code blocks, inset regions. Inverts direction between modes: recessed means darker than the surface in light, and darker still in dark.

inverse.$description: an inverted block, e.g. a tooltip

imageScrim.$description: the veil over a photograph that carries text. Identical in both themes, because the photograph is identical in both themes. Paired with content.onImage, and the pair is gated against the worst case the scrim can sit on rather than against the scrim colour itself - see the audit.

overlayScrim.$description: the veil a modal lays over the page - dialog, drawer, bottom sheet, command palette. Near-black in BOTH themes, so the page behind always goes DARKER. It replaces surface.inverse at opacity.scrim, which in dark mode is a light grey and turned the page grey instead of dimming it (user decision 2026-09-23). The alpha is in the colour: consumers paint it at full opacity. NOT surface.imageScrim, which is a veil under white text on a photograph and is gated on a different question. Gated by the OVERLAY SCRIM gate in build.py: it must darken every theme's page, card and text, and the dialog panel must stay lighter than the page it dims.

inverseSunken.$description: an inset region INSIDE an inverted block: a code chip, a keyboard key, a well. Without it, a code chip on an inverted card keeps its normal-surface fill and renders as a hard black slab on a light inverted card - the loudest thing on a surface whose whole job is to be quiet. Paired with content.inverse, which clears 6.19:1 on it in light and 8.33:1 in dark.

tray.$description: a recessed surface a RAISED control sits on, one step below it: the attachment tray tucked behind a ChatComposer. Neutral 3 in both modes, so it reads as grey and lower than surface.raised in light (#F5F5F5 under white) and in dark (#121212 under #212121). Not surface.sunken, which is neutral 2 in dark and all but vanishes on the black page (2026-09-27).

brandSolid.$description: A brand-coloured surface THAT CARRIES TEXT: table headers, hero panels, filled banners, selected rows. It resolves to the SOLVED brand fill, not the raw brand hex, because white on SSB's literal #1D925B is 3.95:1 and fails AA at normal text sizes - and a 15px table header is normal text, not large. For SST the solved value IS the brand hex (#0245B9 already clears 8.22:1), so nothing changes there; for SSB it is three lightness points deeper, which is the same shift the buttons already take. The literal, locked brand hex still exists untouched at the primitive layer (color.sst.*.9 / color.ssb.*.9) for the logo, illustration and decorative fills - the places where no text sits on it.

disabled.$description: a disabled control's fill. Deliberately one step DEEPER than surface.sunken: it used to resolve to the same #F5F5F5 in light mode, so an inset well and a switched-off control were the same picture. That collision has now been hit three times - the code block reading as disabled, a verifying OTP field reading as disabled, and a sunken chip that could not be told from a dead one - so the two are held apart by the DISTINCT gate in build.py. It also lines up with action.disabled.bg, which was already neutral 4.

code.$description: a code block. It needs its own value because surface.sunken and surface.disabled resolve to the SAME #F5F5F5 in light mode, so a snippet and a switched-off input were the identical grey and the code read as unavailable rather than as code. A code surface is dark in BOTH themes - the convention every developer already has - which also means a snippet never has to be re-syntax-highlighted for a light page.

codeHead.$description: the filename bar above a code block. One step off the block itself, so the two read as one object with a header rather than as two stacked panels.

1.$description: lifted: a control or row lifted under the pointer, a sticky bar edge

3.$description: floating: hover card, floating toolbar, a composer over a conversation

6.$description: dragging: the item held under the pointer

raised.$description: floating layer: popover, menu, toast (= shadow.2)

overlay.$description: modal layer: dialog, drawer, sheet (= shadow.4)

secondary.$description: supporting text, captions, metadata. The quietest text level there is - there is no tertiary.

disabled.$description: text in a disabled control. Exempt from contrast minima.

code.$description: code on surface.code. The light end of whichever ramp the mode uses, because the code surface is dark in both.

codeKeyword.$description: def, return, while - the words the language reserves

codeFunction.$description: a function or method name at its call or definition site

codeComment.$description: a comment. The quietest rung that still clears AA on both code surfaces - a comment that cannot be read is worse than no comment, because the author thinks it is there.

codeHead.$description: the filename and meta in a code block's header. Quieter than the code itself - it is a label on the snippet, not part of it.

inverseSecondary.$description: supporting text, captions and metadata on surface.inverse. Without it an inverted card has exactly one text colour, so a name and the timestamp under it carry equal weight and the hierarchy that exists on every other surface collapses. There is deliberately NO inverseTertiary: the next step down is 5.26:1 in light but 3.44:1 in dark, so it cannot be authored to pass in both, and a third rung that fails half the time is worse than two rungs that always hold.

brand.$description: brand-coloured text. See the philosophy note on when this is allowed.

linkInverse.$description: a link at rest on surface.inverse. It reads the brand ramp of the OPPOSITE mode, because that is the ramp already solved for text on a surface of this lightness. This is the token whose absence is most visible: a link on an inverted card was falling back to content.inverse, which made it the exact colour of the body text beside it, leaving the underline as the only thing saying it was a link.

linkInverseHover.$description: a link being hovered on surface.inverse. One step deeper, the same direction the normal link hover takes.

linkOnBrandSolid.$description: a link on surface.brandSolid. It is WHITE - the same value as content.onBrandSolid - and that is a decision, not an oversight. The tightest brand fill in the system is SSB light, where white itself is only 4.51:1; every tint tested lands below 4.5 (neutral 2 = 4.33, neutral 3 = 4.14). So on a brand fill a link is distinguished by a permanent underline that thickens on hover, never by hue. The token exists so that a link on a brand fill has exactly one legal thing to point at - without it the obvious reach is content.link, which is brand-on-brand and unreadable.

onImage.$description: text on a photograph, over surface.imageScrim. Always white, in every theme and both brands - see the primitive for why a theme-flipping value cannot work here.

onBrandSolid.$description: text on surface.brandSolid. ALWAYS white, on both brands and in both modes - one rule, no exceptions. The surface is chosen to make that legible rather than the label being changed to suit the surface.

decorative.$description: cards, dividers, table rules. NOT an affordance, so it is exempt from the 3:1 rule.

raised.$description: the border of a FLOATING layer - menu, toast, popover, drawer, command palette. In light it is border.decorative and nothing more. In DARK it has to be a step lighter, because those components sit on surface.raised and the decorative border resolves to neutral 6 against a neutral-5 ground: #242424 on #212121, 1.04:1, an invisible edge. Shadows cannot cover for it either - they barely register on black, which is the same reason lightness carries elevation here. Neutral 8 is the user's own live 'strong border' value, so this buys the edge back without inventing a hex. Same shape of fix as surface.raisedHover: the raised layer needs its own pair.

control.$description: inputs, selects, checkboxes. This IS the affordance, so WCAG 1.4.11 applies: >=3:1 against the page. Solved, not guessed.

inert.$description: the unfilled part of a track: a slider rail, a progress trough, a meter's remainder. It has to read as present-but-inactive in BOTH themes, which nothing else in the set does - surface.active is invisible against a dark card, border.decorative nearly so, and border.control is an affordance weight that makes a rail look interactive. It is not an affordance, so the 3:1 rule does not apply to it; what it must not be is absent, because a track with no visible extent gives a filled bar nothing to be a fraction OF.

brand.$description: a brand-coloured edge: a selected card, the active tab, today in a calendar. Step 10 in DARK mode (2026-09-27): step 9 is the locked brand hex in both modes, and on black it was 2.55:1, under the 3:1 a selection indicator needs. Gated against the page, a card and a raised surface in every theme.

focus.$description: the focus ring. 2px wide, 2px offset. Solved to clear 3:1 against every surface it can appear over.

bg.$description: primary button fill. SOLVED against two constraints: label >=4.5:1, and fill >=3:1 against the page so the edge is perceivable.

bgHover.$description: primary button, hovered. One step LIGHTER than rest (user decision 2026-09-23: hover activates, it does not dull). The label drops below 4.5:1 on most themes - a declared exception, see build.py.

bgActive.$description: primary button, pressed. Darker than rest; label and 1.4.11 edge both hold.

borderHover.$description: primary button edge, hovered. One step lighter than the hovered fill: a lit edge. Transparent at rest, so the 1px is reserved and hover causes no layout shift.

fg.$description: primary button label. PAIRED - never override.

bg.$description: secondary button fill

bgHover.$description: secondary button, hovered. A brand WASH, not a greyer grey: in light the old N3 read as dimming, and brand 2 is as luminous as the white rest but chromatic, so it reads as switched on. In dark, brand 6 - brand 4 measured lighter than the N3 rest (0.009 vs 0.006 luminance) but read as a darker navy on screen.

bgActive.$description: secondary button, pressed. DARKER than rest in both modes - in dark the old N5 was lighter than the N3 rest, so pressing brightened the button.

border.$description: secondary button edge. 3:1, because the border is the only thing making it a button.

borderHover.$description: secondary button edge, hovered. A LIGHTER, brand-coloured edge than the grey rest border - the same 'lit edge' the solid buttons get. It is under 3:1 against the page in light; hover is transient and the rest edge carries 1.4.11.

bg.$description: ghost button, no fill at rest

bgHover.$description: ghost button, hovered. Same brand wash as secondary, for the same reason.

bgActive.$description: ghost button, pressed. Darker than hover. In dark nothing is darker than a transparent rest on black, so this is the floor.

borderHover.$description: ghost button edge, hovered. Transparent at rest, so the 1px is reserved.

bg.$description: destructive button fill

bgHover.$description: destructive button, hovered

bgActive.$description: destructive button, pressed

borderHover.$description: destructive button edge, hovered. Lighter than the hovered fill.

bgHover.$description: neutral button, hovered. White in light - brighter than the transparent rest over a subtle region, never a greyer grey. Lighter than the page in dark.

bgActive.$description: neutral button, pressed. Darker than hover.

borderHover.$description: neutral button edge, hovered. Lighter than the rest control border in light; in dark a step lighter than the hovered fill.

bg.$description: any disabled button fill
input fill at rest. White on light; lifted off black in dark.

bgHover.$description: input fill, hovered

bgDisabled.$description: input fill, disabled. Follows surface.disabled exactly - a disabled input and a disabled anything-else are the same state and should not be two greys.

border.$description: input edge at rest. 3:1 - the affordance.

borderHover.$description: input edge, hovered

surface.$description: a soft yellow region: a highlight block, a callout, the wash behind a pulled-out stat. In dark mode this is a deep amber, not a pale one - the region reads as yellow-tinted in both.

border.$description: edge of an accent1 region. This is what gives a yellow fill a perceivable boundary, because the fill itself is only 1.42:1 against a white page and cannot provide one.

content.$description: text on accent1.surface. It is a dark olive, not a yellow, and that is not a bug: a yellow that clears 4.5:1 as text has stopped being yellow. The BRIGHT value lives at accent1.solid, where it is a ground rather than ink.

solid.$description: THE bright yellow. Highlight markers, the one flag on a page, a 'new' pip, the swipe behind a headline word. Same hex in light and dark. It is NOT an action: it has no Action in its name, it fails 1.4.11 against a white page, and it must never be the only thing telling a user something is clickable.

onSolid.$description: the label on accent1.solid. Near-black, in BOTH modes and on BOTH brands, because the fill is the same yellow everywhere. Never white.

surface.$description: the supplied brand wash as a fill. Badges, highlight blocks, callouts. Identical in light and dark - this is how their existing dark pages already use it.

content.$description: orange text. Highlight only, never body copy.

solid.$description: a solid orange fill that can carry a label

onSolid.$description: the label on accent2.solid

ink.$description: text and icons on a photograph's scrim (= content.onImage)

inkSecondary.$description: supporting text on a photograph's scrim. Gated against the worst case, the scrim over white

link.$description: a link on a photograph's scrim

linkHover.$description: a link on a photograph's scrim, hovered (the underline thickens)

fg.$description: label of the white action on a photograph

bgHover.$description: the white action, hovered: a brand wash

bgActive.$description: the white action, pressed

bgHover.$description: an outline or ghost action on a photograph, hovered: an opaque grey the white ink holds on

bgActive.$description: an outline or ghost action on a photograph, pressed

surface.$description: a glass control's tint on the page (mode-aware)
a glass control's white frost over a photograph's scrim

highlight.$description: the light on glass: the sheen and the rim. White in every mode, because light does not change colour with the theme

onSolid.$description: label on the solid success fill
label on the solid warning fill
label on the solid danger fill
label on the solid info fill

label on the solid warning fill
label on the solid danger fill
label on the solid info fill

page.$description: the page itself. White in light, true black in dark - the user's own shipping value.

subtle.$description: a quietly differentiated region on the page

default.$description: cards and panels. NOTE the asymmetry, and it is deliberate: in LIGHT mode a card is the SAME white as the page and is separated by its border - that is what borders-over-shadows means, and it is what their references actually do. In DARK mode a card is LIGHTER than the page, because shadows do not register on black and lightness has to carry elevation instead. This is why dark mode is authored as a second value set and never as an inversion.

active.$description: a surface being pressed or selected

raised.$description: popovers, menus, dialogs. Lighter again in dark mode - one more elevation step.

raisedHover.$description: a row or control being hovered ON a raised surface. surface.hover cannot do this job in dark mode: it resolves to neutral 4, which is DARKER than surface.raised at neutral 5, so a menu item hovered on a popover got quieter instead of louder and surface.active is the same value as the surface itself. Elevation reverses the direction a hover has to move in, which is exactly why dark mode is authored rather than inverted, and why the raised layer needs its own pair.

raisedActive.$description: a row or control being pressed on a raised surface

sunken.$description: wells, code blocks, inset regions. Inverts direction between modes: recessed means darker than the surface in light, and darker still in dark.

inverse.$description: an inverted block, e.g. a tooltip

imageScrim.$description: the veil over a photograph that carries text. Identical in both themes, because the photograph is identical in both themes. Paired with content.onImage, and the pair is gated against the worst case the scrim can sit on rather than against the scrim colour itself - see the audit.

overlayScrim.$description: the veil a modal lays over the page - dialog, drawer, bottom sheet, command palette. Near-black in BOTH themes, so the page behind always goes DARKER. It replaces surface.inverse at opacity.scrim, which in dark mode is a light grey and turned the page grey instead of dimming it (user decision 2026-09-23). The alpha is in the colour: consumers paint it at full opacity. NOT surface.imageScrim, which is a veil under white text on a photograph and is gated on a different question. Gated by the OVERLAY SCRIM gate in build.py: it must darken every theme's page, card and text, and the dialog panel must stay lighter than the page it dims.

inverseSunken.$description: an inset region INSIDE an inverted block: a code chip, a keyboard key, a well. Without it, a code chip on an inverted card keeps its normal-surface fill and renders as a hard black slab on a light inverted card - the loudest thing on a surface whose whole job is to be quiet. Paired with content.inverse, which clears 6.19:1 on it in light and 8.33:1 in dark.

tray.$description: a recessed surface a RAISED control sits on, one step below it: the attachment tray tucked behind a ChatComposer. Neutral 3 in both modes, so it reads as grey and lower than surface.raised in light (#F5F5F5 under white) and in dark (#121212 under #212121). Not surface.sunken, which is neutral 2 in dark and all but vanishes on the black page (2026-09-27).

brandSolid.$description: A brand-coloured surface THAT CARRIES TEXT: table headers, hero panels, filled banners, selected rows. It resolves to the SOLVED brand fill, not the raw brand hex, because white on SSB's literal #1D925B is 3.95:1 and fails AA at normal text sizes - and a 15px table header is normal text, not large. For SST the solved value IS the brand hex (#0245B9 already clears 8.22:1), so nothing changes there; for SSB it is three lightness points deeper, which is the same shift the buttons already take. The literal, locked brand hex still exists untouched at the primitive layer (color.sst.*.9 / color.ssb.*.9) for the logo, illustration and decorative fills - the places where no text sits on it.

disabled.$description: a disabled control's fill. Deliberately one step DEEPER than surface.sunken: it used to resolve to the same #F5F5F5 in light mode, so an inset well and a switched-off control were the same picture. That collision has now been hit three times - the code block reading as disabled, a verifying OTP field reading as disabled, and a sunken chip that could not be told from a dead one - so the two are held apart by the DISTINCT gate in build.py. It also lines up with action.disabled.bg, which was already neutral 4.

code.$description: a code block. It needs its own value because surface.sunken and surface.disabled resolve to the SAME #F5F5F5 in light mode, so a snippet and a switched-off input were the identical grey and the code read as unavailable rather than as code. A code surface is dark in BOTH themes - the convention every developer already has - which also means a snippet never has to be re-syntax-highlighted for a light page.

codeHead.$description: the filename bar above a code block. One step off the block itself, so the two read as one object with a header rather than as two stacked panels.

1.$description: lifted: a control or row lifted under the pointer, a sticky bar edge

3.$description: floating: hover card, floating toolbar, a composer over a conversation

6.$description: dragging: the item held under the pointer

raised.$description: floating layer: popover, menu, toast (= shadow.2)

overlay.$description: modal layer: dialog, drawer, sheet (= shadow.4)

secondary.$description: supporting text, captions, metadata. The quietest text level there is - there is no tertiary.

disabled.$description: text in a disabled control. Exempt from contrast minima.

code.$description: code on surface.code. The light end of whichever ramp the mode uses, because the code surface is dark in both.

codeKeyword.$description: def, return, while - the words the language reserves

codeFunction.$description: a function or method name at its call or definition site

codeComment.$description: a comment. The quietest rung that still clears AA on both code surfaces - a comment that cannot be read is worse than no comment, because the author thinks it is there.

codeHead.$description: the filename and meta in a code block's header. Quieter than the code itself - it is a label on the snippet, not part of it.

inverseSecondary.$description: supporting text, captions and metadata on surface.inverse. Without it an inverted card has exactly one text colour, so a name and the timestamp under it carry equal weight and the hierarchy that exists on every other surface collapses. There is deliberately NO inverseTertiary: the next step down is 5.26:1 in light but 3.44:1 in dark, so it cannot be authored to pass in both, and a third rung that fails half the time is worse than two rungs that always hold.

brand.$description: brand-coloured text. See the philosophy note on when this is allowed.

linkInverse.$description: a link at rest on surface.inverse. It reads the brand ramp of the OPPOSITE mode, because that is the ramp already solved for text on a surface of this lightness. This is the token whose absence is most visible: a link on an inverted card was falling back to content.inverse, which made it the exact colour of the body text beside it, leaving the underline as the only thing saying it was a link.

linkInverseHover.$description: a link being hovered on surface.inverse. One step deeper, the same direction the normal link hover takes.

linkOnBrandSolid.$description: a link on surface.brandSolid. It is WHITE - the same value as content.onBrandSolid - and that is a decision, not an oversight. The tightest brand fill in the system is SSB light, where white itself is only 4.51:1; every tint tested lands below 4.5 (neutral 2 = 4.33, neutral 3 = 4.14). So on a brand fill a link is distinguished by a permanent underline that thickens on hover, never by hue. The token exists so that a link on a brand fill has exactly one legal thing to point at - without it the obvious reach is content.link, which is brand-on-brand and unreadable.

onImage.$description: text on a photograph, over surface.imageScrim. Always white, in every theme and both brands - see the primitive for why a theme-flipping value cannot work here.

onBrandSolid.$description: text on surface.brandSolid. ALWAYS white, on both brands and in both modes - one rule, no exceptions. The surface is chosen to make that legible rather than the label being changed to suit the surface.

decorative.$description: cards, dividers, table rules. NOT an affordance, so it is exempt from the 3:1 rule.

raised.$description: the border of a FLOATING layer - menu, toast, popover, drawer, command palette. In light it is border.decorative and nothing more. In DARK it has to be a step lighter, because those components sit on surface.raised and the decorative border resolves to neutral 6 against a neutral-5 ground: #242424 on #212121, 1.04:1, an invisible edge. Shadows cannot cover for it either - they barely register on black, which is the same reason lightness carries elevation here. Neutral 8 is the user's own live 'strong border' value, so this buys the edge back without inventing a hex. Same shape of fix as surface.raisedHover: the raised layer needs its own pair.

control.$description: inputs, selects, checkboxes. This IS the affordance, so WCAG 1.4.11 applies: >=3:1 against the page. Solved, not guessed.

inert.$description: the unfilled part of a track: a slider rail, a progress trough, a meter's remainder. It has to read as present-but-inactive in BOTH themes, which nothing else in the set does - surface.active is invisible against a dark card, border.decorative nearly so, and border.control is an affordance weight that makes a rail look interactive. It is not an affordance, so the 3:1 rule does not apply to it; what it must not be is absent, because a track with no visible extent gives a filled bar nothing to be a fraction OF.

brand.$description: a brand-coloured edge: a selected card, the active tab, today in a calendar. Step 10 in DARK mode (2026-09-27): step 9 is the locked brand hex in both modes, and on black it was 2.55:1, under the 3:1 a selection indicator needs. Gated against the page, a card and a raised surface in every theme.

focus.$description: the focus ring. 2px wide, 2px offset. Solved to clear 3:1 against every surface it can appear over.

bg.$description: primary button fill. SOLVED against two constraints: label >=4.5:1, and fill >=3:1 against the page so the edge is perceivable.

bgHover.$description: primary button, hovered. One step LIGHTER than rest (user decision 2026-09-23: hover activates, it does not dull). The label drops below 4.5:1 on most themes - a declared exception, see build.py.

bgActive.$description: primary button, pressed. Darker than rest; label and 1.4.11 edge both hold.

borderHover.$description: primary button edge, hovered. One step lighter than the hovered fill: a lit edge. Transparent at rest, so the 1px is reserved and hover causes no layout shift.

fg.$description: primary button label. PAIRED - never override.

bg.$description: secondary button fill

bgHover.$description: secondary button, hovered. A brand WASH, not a greyer grey: in light the old N3 read as dimming, and brand 2 is as luminous as the white rest but chromatic, so it reads as switched on. In dark, brand 6 - brand 4 measured lighter than the N3 rest (0.009 vs 0.006 luminance) but read as a darker navy on screen.

bgActive.$description: secondary button, pressed. DARKER than rest in both modes - in dark the old N5 was lighter than the N3 rest, so pressing brightened the button.

border.$description: secondary button edge. 3:1, because the border is the only thing making it a button.

borderHover.$description: secondary button edge, hovered. A LIGHTER, brand-coloured edge than the grey rest border - the same 'lit edge' the solid buttons get. It is under 3:1 against the page in light; hover is transient and the rest edge carries 1.4.11.

bg.$description: ghost button, no fill at rest

bgHover.$description: ghost button, hovered. Same brand wash as secondary, for the same reason.

bgActive.$description: ghost button, pressed. Darker than hover. In dark nothing is darker than a transparent rest on black, so this is the floor.

borderHover.$description: ghost button edge, hovered. Transparent at rest, so the 1px is reserved.

bg.$description: destructive button fill

bgHover.$description: destructive button, hovered

bgActive.$description: destructive button, pressed

borderHover.$description: destructive button edge, hovered. Lighter than the hovered fill.

bgHover.$description: neutral button, hovered. White in light - brighter than the transparent rest over a subtle region, never a greyer grey. Lighter than the page in dark.

bgActive.$description: neutral button, pressed. Darker than hover.

borderHover.$description: neutral button edge, hovered. Lighter than the rest control border in light; in dark a step lighter than the hovered fill.

bg.$description: any disabled button fill
input fill at rest. White on light; lifted off black in dark.

bgHover.$description: input fill, hovered

bgDisabled.$description: input fill, disabled. Follows surface.disabled exactly - a disabled input and a disabled anything-else are the same state and should not be two greys.

border.$description: input edge at rest. 3:1 - the affordance.

borderHover.$description: input edge, hovered

surface.$description: a soft yellow region: a highlight block, a callout, the wash behind a pulled-out stat. In dark mode this is a deep amber, not a pale one - the region reads as yellow-tinted in both.

border.$description: edge of an accent1 region. This is what gives a yellow fill a perceivable boundary, because the fill itself is only 1.42:1 against a white page and cannot provide one.

content.$description: text on accent1.surface. It is a dark olive, not a yellow, and that is not a bug: a yellow that clears 4.5:1 as text has stopped being yellow. The BRIGHT value lives at accent1.solid, where it is a ground rather than ink.

solid.$description: THE bright yellow. Highlight markers, the one flag on a page, a 'new' pip, the swipe behind a headline word. Same hex in light and dark. It is NOT an action: it has no Action in its name, it fails 1.4.11 against a white page, and it must never be the only thing telling a user something is clickable.

onSolid.$description: the label on accent1.solid. Near-black, in BOTH modes and on BOTH brands, because the fill is the same yellow everywhere. Never white.

surface.$description: the supplied brand wash as a fill. Badges, highlight blocks, callouts. Identical in light and dark - this is how their existing dark pages already use it.

content.$description: orange text. Highlight only, never body copy.

solid.$description: a solid orange fill that can carry a label

onSolid.$description: the label on accent2.solid

ink.$description: text and icons on a photograph's scrim (= content.onImage)

inkSecondary.$description: supporting text on a photograph's scrim. Gated against the worst case, the scrim over white

link.$description: a link on a photograph's scrim

linkHover.$description: a link on a photograph's scrim, hovered (the underline thickens)

fg.$description: label of the white action on a photograph

bgHover.$description: the white action, hovered: a brand wash

bgActive.$description: the white action, pressed

bgHover.$description: an outline or ghost action on a photograph, hovered: an opaque grey the white ink holds on

bgActive.$description: an outline or ghost action on a photograph, pressed

surface.$description: a glass control's tint on the page (mode-aware)
